pg012_p020: Proteins are organic compounds made up of one or more chains of amino acids.
pg012_p022: Amino acids are made of smaller units that contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur. There are two groups of amino acids: essential amino acids and non-essential amino acids.
pg012_p027: The essential amino acids are obtained from foods eaten, while non-essential amino acids can be made by the body.
pg012_p030: However, the body cannot produce essential amino acids. Foods like beef, chicken, fish, termites, eggs, beans, lentils, peas, groundnuts, mushrooms, and milk and its products like cheese are rich in proteins hence provide essential amino acids. Figure 1.3 shows examples of foods that are sources of proteins.
pg012_im001: Protein-rich foods including meat, chicken, fish, beans, eggs, cheese, and a glass of milk.
pg012_p041: Proteins have several functions in the human body including building body cells, promoting growth, and making protoplasm. Proteins also help to repair damaged tissues such as replacing damaged or lost cells in wounds, skin, and mucus membranes. Since proteins are major components of all cell membranes, they play a role in the transport of other molecules across the cell membranes. They form part of the cell structure, and aid in the contraction of muscles. They are sometimes used as a source of energy, especially when the body lacks carbohydrates and lipids. Each gram of protein provides four kilocalories (kcal) of energy.
pg012_p058: However, proteins are not the major source of energy in the body. Their primary function is to promote growth and repair worn out body tissues.
pg012_p062: Proteins are essential for growing children, pregnant women, and people recovering from illnesses.
pg013_p003: When proteins are consumed, they are broken down into amino acids that are absorbed into the bloodstream and used by the body to produce its own proteins.
pg013_p007: For example, the haemoglobin found in the red blood cells is one of the body proteins. Haemoglobin enables red blood cells to transport oxygen in our bodies. Other examples of body proteins include antibodies which provide body immunity and enzymes that are involved in food digestion. In addition, many hormones are protein in nature. They control and regulate various processes in the body.

pg020_p033: Sweating is one of the means by which water prevents the human body from overheating during hot weather. This is because evaporation of sweat from the surface of the skin helps the body to cool during hot conditions. pg022_p046: Pregnant women and lactating mothers need to get enough nutrients in their meals. pg023_p044: Young children are still growing and they are generally most active. They require diets that provide them with adequate nutrients to ensure proper functioning of their bodies. They need enough proteins for growth and development of the body tissues.

pg025_p013: It is advisable to use the food guide pyramid in determining what to eat.
pg025_p015: The food guide pyramid is a chart showing the recommended amounts of variety of foods that dieticians consider as healthy for eating. Figure 1.8 shows an example of a food guide pyramid.
pg025_p020: It is not a fixed rule of what to eat each day, but just a general guide that helps to choose the right healthy diet. It helps an individual to eat better every day. The base constitutes foods that are required in larger amounts while the apex constitutes foods that need to be taken in lesser amounts. The food guide pyramid is not universal for all groups of people, it depends on the needs and health status of a person. pg044_p008: The human digestive system is composed of the alimentary canal, associated organs, and glands as shown in Figure 2.1. The main parts of the alimentary canal are the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The small intestine comprises the duodenum and ileum, whereas the large intestine comprises the colon, rectum and anal canal. The associated organs include the tongue, liver, pancreas, gall bladder and appendix. The digestive system also contains the salivary glands.
pg044_p017: Food taken into the body cannot be utilised by the cells unless it is broken down and changed into simpler, soluble, and diffusible form. Digestion takes place in the alimentary canal. In this chapter, you will learn about nutrition in human and ruminants including their digestive systems and digestion processes. The competences developed will enable you to practise a proper eating habit to avoid disorders and diseases associated with the digestive system.

pg047_p018: Teeth facilitate the chewing of food in the mouth. Chewing is necessary because it breaks down large particles of food into smaller particles and mixes the food particles with saliva for easy swallowing. The presence of food in the mouth stimulates the salivary glands to release more saliva. Saliva contains a digestive enzyme called salivary amylase (ptyalin) that catalyses the break down of cooked starch into maltose. Saliva in the mouth also helps to moisten the mouth, tongue and lips.

pg047_p033: After the food has been chewed, it is rolled by the tongue into small balls called boli (singular bolus). The teeth, saliva, and tongue play important roles in rolling the food into the bolus. In this form, the food is ready to be swallowed via the pharynx and oesophagus.
pg047_p040: During swallowing, the food bolus is pressed against the roof of the mouth and pushed into the pharynx by the muscular action of the tongue. The pharynx is the cavity behind the mouth, which is connected to the stomach by the oesophagus. It is also connected to the nostrils or air pathways by the nasal cavity. Furthermore, the pharynx is connected to the ears by the eustachian tubes and to the trachea by the epiglottis. Epiglottis is a flap of cartilage that controls entry of air into the trachea. It opens to allow air to enter the lungs through the trachea. When eating food, the epiglottis closes the trachea to prevent food from entering the air passage. After the bolus has entered the oesophagus, the epiglottis opens again to allow air to pass into the trachea and proceeds down to the lungs. From the pharynx, food goes into the oesophagus. pg074_p010: Osmosis is an important process in both plants and animals. In plants, osmosis aids the absorption of water by the roots. Osmosis also aids the opening and closing of the stomata. When guard cells absorb water the stomata open. When they lose water, the stomata close. Osmosis also plays a key role during seed germination. It enables the absorption of water that softens the seed coat, hence, increasing seed permeability for dissolved minerals and oxygen. This promotes the growth of seed embryo during germination.

pg075_p003: In animal cells, osmosis is important for reabsorption of water in the colon and kidneys. This process helps to maintain water balance in the body. In addition, the process of osmosis is used to preserve food by salting. This causes food such as meat to lose water and become dry. Salting makes food to stay longer without being contaminated by germs.
pg075_p013: In lower organisms such as Amoeba, osmosis helps to remove waste and excess water from their bodies.
pg075_p016: Effects of osmosis in living organisms
pg075_p017: Osmosis is one of the most important processes that help to keep the organisms body conditions stable for their survival. However, the process of osmosis has various effects in the cells of living things as described below.
pg075_p023: Osmosis in animal cells: Animal cells take in and lose water by the process of osmosis. However, when an animal cell is put in a hypotonic solution, it absorbs water. If it remains in the solution for a long time, it absorbs excess amounts of water. A cell that does not have a mechanism for removing excess water bursts due to its excessive internal pressure.
pg075_p033: When an animal cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, it loses water. If it remains in the solution for a long
pg075_p036: time, it loses a lot of water, shrinks, and shrivels. These effects of osmosis on animal cells can be observed in red blood cells. Under normal conditions, the osmotic pressure of red blood cells is equal to that of the blood plasma implying that they are isotonic. Thus, there is equal movement of water in and out of the cells. This helps to maintain the disc shape of these cells.
pg075_p046: When red blood cells are placed in a hypotonic solution, they absorb water, causing the cell volume to increase.
pg075_p049: Excessive amounts of water cause haemolysis (bursting).
pg075_p051: When red blood cells are placed in a hypertonic solution, they lose water, leading to shrinking of the cell. This is referred to as crenation (Figure 3.5).

pg091_p005: Root hairs are extensions of the epidermal cells of the root. Figure 4.12 shows the structure of a root hair.

pg091_p015: Root hairs are long and slender to provide a large surface area for the absorption of water and mineral salts from the soil. The large number of root hairs increases the total surface area of the roots for the absorption of water and mineral salts. Root hairs contain vacuoles filled with cell sap. The root hair cell sap is usually hypertonic; that is, more concentrated than the surrounding water. Hence, water enters the root hair cells by osmosis. They have permeable cell walls which are hydrophilic in nature.
pg091_p030: root hairs are always in search of water supply. If root hair cells have a higher concentration of mineral salts than their surroundings, mineral salts are absorbed by active transport. Root hairs are very thin to provide a short distance over which the absorbed water and mineral salts have to travel to reach the cell.
pg091_p039: As the main roots elongate, the older root hairs die and are replaced with new ones. This helps the plant to have a constant supply of water and mineral salts from the soil.

The pulmonary artery transports deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. pg107_p024: The heart is an organ that pumps blood throughout the body. It is divided into two separate pumping systems, the right side and the left side. The right side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the vena cava and pumps it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen gas and releases carbon dioxide gas. The left side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it through the arteries to the rest of the body, where oxygen gas is released and
pg107_p036: carbon dioxide gas is picked up. Apart from transporting gases, the blood also transports nutrients and water needed in the metabolic processes of the body.
pg107_p040: Deoxygenated blood has a high concentration of carbon dioxide. The vena cava has two branches that are superior vena cava and inferior vena cava. The superior vena cava transports deoxygenated blood from the upper parts of the body such as the head, neck, and upper limbs to the heart.
pg107_p048: The inferior vena cava transports deoxygenated blood from the lower parts of the body such as the lower limbs, kidney, liver, stomach, and intestines to the heart. The inferior vena cava and the superior vena cava, unite to form the vena cava that connects to the right auricle.
pg107_p056: The right auricle receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve. When the right auricle relaxes, it is filled up with deoxygenated blood from the vena cava. The increased pressure in the right auricle causes muscles to contract and pump the blood through the tricuspid valve. In the right auricle, there is a small patch of muscle called the sinoatrial node (SAN). This node acts as a pacemaker, setting the time and rate of cardiac muscle
pg108_p003: contraction. When muscles of the right ventricle relax, the ventricle is filled up with blood. The tricuspid valve closes to prevent blood from flowing back into the right auricle.
pg108_p008: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. When the right ventricle is full, the increased pressure causes the muscles to contract, and the semilunar valve in the pulmonary artery to open. Blood flows into the pulmonary artery, and the semilunar valve closes to prevent back flow of blood. The pulmonary artery transports deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, and thus becomes oxygenated.
pg108_p021: The oxygenated blood flows from the lungs to the heart through the pulmonary vein. This vein is connected to the left auricle. When the left auricle relaxes, blood from the pulmonary vein flows into it. Pressure increases in the left auricle as it fills up with blood which causes the muscles of the auricle to contract and pump blood through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle.
pg108_p031: The muscles of the left ventricle relax, allowing blood to flow in. The bicuspid valve closes to prevent blood from flowing back into the left auricle.
pg108_p035: Pressure builds up in the left ventricle as blood flows in. The muscles of the left ventricle contract, pumping blood through the semilunar valve into the aorta. The aorta branches into smaller arteries that transport blood to all parts of the body.
pg108_p042: The heart beats in such a way that when the auricles contract, the ventricles relax and vice versa. Usually an adult heart beats about 60 to 80 times per minute. A baby’s heart beats faster than the adult heart, about 70 to 190 beats per minute because babies have higher metabolic rates than adults.

qz001_que: Animals are called heterotrophs because they get food from what?
qz001_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Animals cannot make their own food, so they depend on other organisms for nutrients.
qz001_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Sunlight is used by autotrophs like green plants to make food, but animals do not make food this way.
qz001_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Animals need food nutrients from plants or other animals, not just air.
qz002_que: What is the main function of proteins in the body?
qz002_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Lipids provide the most energy, not proteins.
qz002_o1_exp: ❌ Not exactly. Fat under the skin helps reduce heat loss, but that is not the main function of proteins.
qz002_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Proteins mainly help the body grow and repair worn-out or damaged tissues.
qz003_que: What is the main function of carbohydrates in the body?
qz003_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Blood clotting is mainly linked with vitamin K, not carbohydrates.
qz003_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Carbohydrates are the body's major source of energy and are broken down into glucose to fuel body cells.
qz003_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Building and maintaining bones is mainly helped by vitamins such as vitamin D.
qz004_que: Which mineral helps the body make thyroid hormone?
qz004_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Calcium mainly helps build strong bones and teeth and helps with nerve transmission and muscle contraction.
qz004_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Iron is mainly needed to make haemoglobin, the red pigment in blood.
qz004_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Iodine is needed for the production of thyroid hormone, which helps regulate growth, development, and metabolism.
qz005_o0: 1) A meal with only fruits and water
qz005_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Fruits and water are important, but a balanced diet includes all food groups, not only these two.
qz005_o1: 2) A meal with a lot of sugar and fat
qz005_o1_exp: ❌ No. The text advises limiting too much sugar and fat for a healthy lifestyle.
qz005_o2: 3) A meal with all food groups in the right proportions
qz005_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! The text says a balanced diet contains foods from all food groups in the right proportions.
qz006_que: Which nutrient do children need for growth and development of body tissues?

qz006_o2_exp: ❌ Not right. Alcohol is harmful, especially for pregnant women and babies, and it does not help children grow.

qz016_que: In osmosis, water moves through a partially permeable membrane from a ____ solution to a ____ solution.
qz016_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. In osmosis, water moves from where there is more water and less solute to where there is less water and more solute.
qz016_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Water moves from a hypotonic solution to a hypertonic solution through a partially permeable membrane.
qz016_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Isotonic solutions have equal concentration, so there is no net movement of water in one direction.
qz017_que: What is a plant cell called after it loses water in a hypertonic solution?

qz017_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Isotonic describes a condition where there is no net gain or loss of water.

qz020_que: How are vascular bundles arranged in a dicot stem?

qz020_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. Parallel arrangement is used to describe veins in monocot leaves, not vascular bundles in dicot stems.
qz020_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring around the central pith.
qz021_que: Why are root hairs long and slender?
qz021_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Root hairs help with absorption from the soil, not with making flowers bright.
qz021_o1_exp: ❌ Good try. Water vapour is mainly released through stomata in the leaves, not by root hairs.
qz021_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Root hairs are long and slender so they have a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts from the soil.
qz022_que: Through which part do plants lose most water during transpiration?
qz022_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Xylem transports water through the plant, but it is not the main place where water leaves the plant.
qz022_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Plants lose most water through the stomata, which are tiny openings in the leaves.
qz022_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Roots mainly absorb water from the soil rather than lose most of it.
qz023_que: Through which structure does guttation mainly take place?
qz023_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Guttation happens through hydathodes, which release drops of liquid water at the leaf edges or tips.
qz023_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Roots absorb water from the soil, but guttation comes out through special leaf openings, not the roots.
qz023_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Stomata are mainly involved in transpiration, where water is lost as vapour.
qz024_que: What is the main function of the mammalian heart?
qz024_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Making food is done by green plants during photosynthesis, not by the heart.
qz024_o1_exp: ❌ Try again. Absorbing water is a job of plant roots, not the mammalian heart.
qz024_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! The mammalian heart pumps blood throughout the body through blood vessels.
qz025_que: What is the main function of heart valves?
qz025_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. The heart muscles and chambers pump blood, while valves help control where the blood goes.
qz025_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. The septum prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
qz025_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Heart valves make sure blood flows in only one direction and does not flow backward.
qz026_que: What is the main function of capillaries?
qz026_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Capillaries exchange oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide, and other wastes between the blood and body cells.
qz026_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Valves in veins help prevent blood from flowing backward.
qz026_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. The heart pumps blood, not capillaries.
qz027_que: Which blood cells help the body fight diseases and infections?
qz027_o0_exp: ❌ Not correct. Platelets mainly help blood to clot, not fight infections.
qz027_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Red blood cells mainly transport oxygen and carbon dioxide.
qz027_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! White blood cells protect the body against diseases and infections.
qz028_que: What type of blood circulation do human beings have?
qz028_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Single circulation happens in less complex organisms like fish, where blood passes through the heart once in one complete circuit.
qz028_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Human beings have double circulation, meaning blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circulation.
qz028_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. The passage explains pulmonary and systemic circulation in humans, which together make double circulation.
qz029_que: What is one main importance of blood circulation in the body?
qz029_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Blood circulation carries oxygen and other needed substances to body tissues.
qz029_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. Digestion happens in the digestive system, while blood circulation moves substances like oxygen, nutrients, and wastes.
qz029_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Bones are not made by blood circulation. The passage explains that blood mainly transports materials around the body.
qz030_que: What is one way to help prevent arteriosclerosis?
qz030_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! The text says regular physical exercise helps reduce the chance of developing arteriosclerosis.
qz030_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. Too much fat in the diet increases the risk of arteriosclerosis.
qz030_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Smoking is listed as a cause of arteriosclerosis, not a way to prevent it.

qz031_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Gas exchange is the process where oxygen enters the body and carbon dioxide leaves across a respiratory surface.
qz031_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Pumping blood is the work of the circulatory system, not the meaning of gas exchange.
qz031_o2: 3) Breaking down food in the stomach
qz031_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Breaking down food is part of digestion, not gas exchange.
qz032_que: What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation?
qz032_o0: 1) It traps dust in the nose
qz032_o0_exp: ❌ Not correct. Trapping dust is the job of mucus in the nasal cavity, not the diaphragm.
qz032_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, making more space in the thorax so air can enter the lungs.
qz032_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped during exhalation, not inhalation.
qz033_que: Where does the actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide take place in the lungs?
qz033_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. The trachea is the windpipe that carries air, but gas exchange does not happen there.
qz033_o1_exp: ❌ Not exactly. The pharynx is part of the air passage, but it is not where gases are exchanged.
qz033_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! The alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
qz034_que: Which part of a leaf mainly allows gases to move in and out?
qz034_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Roots mainly absorb water and minerals from the soil, not gas exchange in the leaf.
qz034_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Stomata are tiny pores on leaves that allow gas exchange between the plant and the air.
qz034_o2_exp: ❌ Not correct. Flowers are mainly for reproduction, not the main place where leaf gas exchange happens.
qz035_que: Anaerobic respiration takes place in the absence of what?
qz035_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Water may be involved in life processes, but anaerobic respiration is defined by the absence of oxygen.
qz035_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. Carbon dioxide can be produced during respiration, but anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is absent.
qz035_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Anaerobic respiration happens when there is no oxygen available.
qz036_que: What is produced in animals during anaerobic respiration?
qz036_o0_exp: ❌ Not correct. Oxygen is not produced during respiration; it is used in aerobic respiration.
qz036_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! In animals, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid and energy.
qz036_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Water is produced in aerobic respiration, not in anaerobic respiration in animals.
qz037_que: Which vaccine is given to children to help prevent tuberculosis?
qz037_o0_exp: ❌ Not correct. Nicotine is a harmful substance in cigarette smoke and does not prevent tuberculosis.
qz037_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! The text says the Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine is given to children to prevent tuberculosis.
qz037_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. SARS-CoV-2 is the virus that causes COVID-19, not a vaccine for tuberculosis.
qz038_que: What is the movement of molecules from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration called?
qz038_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Digestion is the breakdown of food into simpler forms that can be absorbed by the body.
qz038_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. Excretion is the removal of harmful waste products from the body.
qz038_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Diffusion is the movement of molecules or ions from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
qz039_que: Which process helps green plants make their own food?
qz039_o0_exp: ❌ Not quite. Respiration releases energy from food inside cells, but it does not make food for plants.
qz039_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food using carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight energy.
qz039_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Osmosis is the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane, not food-making.
qz040_que: Which plant tissue transports water and minerals in vascular plants?
qz040_o0_exp: ✅ Correct! Xylem is the tissue that transports water and minerals in vascular plants.
qz040_o1_exp: ❌ Not quite. Villi are finger-like projections in the ileum that help absorb food, not plant transport tissue.
qz040_o2_exp: ❌ Try again. A vein carries blood to the heart in animals, not water in plants.
qz041_que: Which plant tissue transports food in a plant?
qz041_o0_exp: ❌ Good try. Tracheids mainly help transport water and support the plant, not food.
qz041_o1_exp: ✅ Correct! Phloem transports food made by the plant from the leaves to other parts.
qz041_o2_exp: ❌ Not quite. Stomata are tiny openings on leaves that help with gas exchange, not food transport.
